source: GitHub Advisory OSV + GitHub Advisory API (malicious package detection)
description: Open-source supply-chain attacks: malicious npm/pypi packages with preinstall hooks, dependency confusion, credential exfiltration, or remote code execution payloads.

The gem declares ext/mkrf_conf.rb as a native extension, which causes RubyGems to execute it during `gem install`. The script performs no native build activity (no mkmf calls, no Rakefile emission, no C/C++ sources are shipped). Instead it collects the installer's hostname, username, current working directory, home directory, and the contents of /etc/passwd, /etc/hosts, and /etc/resolv.conf, serializes them as JSON, and transmits them over a TLS TCP socket to geymj1lxqj2u1nzkaqe6zrg33u9yxold.oastify.com:443 (a Burp Collaborator subdomain), with a DNS probe to the same host. The package name mimics the legitimate TDesign Vue component family, but the shipped code is purely an install-time reconnaissance and exfiltration payload.

The OpenSSF Package Analysis project identified 'tdesign-vue-mono' @ 1.0.1 (rubygems) as malicious.

It is considered malicious because:

- The package communicates with a domain associated with malicious activity.

setup.py overrides the build_py command so that during sdist install it calls hello.fetch(), which downloads hello.bat from raw.githubusercontent.com/misdry01/bookish-octo-lamp/refs/heads/main/hello.bat (a personal GitHub account on the mutable main branch, no pinning, no hash or signature check) and launches it via subprocess.Popen(['cmd.exe','/d','/c', path], creationflags=CREATE_NO_WINDOW), hiding the window. The wheel's bdist_wheel override additionally writes a qap793gl4l_boot.pth file containing 'import qap793gl4l_boot' into the site-packages root, so on every subsequent interpreter start site.py auto-imports qap793gl4l_boot, which re-invokes hello.fetch() and runs the remote batch file the same way. A temp-directory marker gates execution to once per machine but is trivially deletable, making the channel re-armable. vmcheck.py also implements DMI-based VM/sandbox detection, and update() refuses to run inside detected VMs via VMBlockedError, which is analyst-evasion scaffolding consistent with the dropper. The author controls the bytes served from the mutable URL and can change them at any time without republishing the package.

Continuation of a campaign executing remote code. During analysis of this package, the remote Github repository did not yet host the malicious code.

The sole module shipped in both the sdist and the wheel, main.py, consists entirely of `exec(zlib.decompress(base64.b85decode('...')))` at the top level. The package exposes this module as `py_modules=['main']` and wires it as the `psbool` console_script, so the opaque, compressed-and-encoded blob is decoded and executed unconditionally the first time the module is imported or the CLI is invoked. There is no source, documentation, or API surface — the entire implementation is a single encoded payload, deliberately concealing its behavior from anyone inspecting the package before it runs. A boolean-logic utility has no legitimate reason to ship its implementation as an opaque exec-of-decoded-bytes blob; this is the canonical obfuscated-payload import-time execution shape and causes an arbitrary author-controlled program to run on the installer's machine.

During import, obfuscated code exfiltrates photos and documents to a Telegram bot. It targets Android devices.

setup.py defines a custom install cmdclass (PostInstall) that runs exec(base64.b64decode(...).decode()) during `pip install`. The decoded payload enumerates classic installer secrets — ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.env — and cryptocurrency wallet stores (Ethereum keystore, Exodus, MetaMask, Solana, Phantom), plus matching *.json files, base64-encodes portions of each file, and POSTs them to a hardcoded Discord webhook at discord.com/api/webhooks/1570872953443455097/. The base64+exec wrapper exists only to hide the stealer from casual review of setup.py.

The package's postinstall script downloads an executable from http://185.212.128.180/chromedriver.bat, writes it to ~/.celest/bin/chrome (or chrome.exe), sets it executable, and later launches it through puppeteer-core. The source is a bare IPv4 address over plain HTTP with no hash, signature, or version pinning, and the URL path is a Windows.bat named 'chromedriver' while the package frames the artifact as a patched Chromium. The same download-and-execute path is also reached from src/browser.js, which calls download() followed by puppeteer.launch({ executablePath }) on first library use, so require()/import of the package will fetch and run the binary even when the postinstall step is skipped via CELEST_SKIP_DOWNLOAD. The destination host is not associated with any legitimate Chromium publisher, and the operator of that host fully controls the bytes that are executed on the installer's machine.
